title: The Skykeeper and the Star Eater
subtitle: A disappearing sky leads to a surprising act of compassion.
editorialNote: New story adapted from a recovered plot summary; original wording was unavailable.

paragraphs: The first missing star left a little dark hole above the galaxy tent.
The second took the light from the cushion path.
By the time Opal reached the village square, a whole corner of the sky had gone quiet.
A Skykeeper stood beside the lantern tree, holding an empty basket woven from moonlight.
“The Star Eater is coming,” she said.
Langston looked upward. “Has anyone offered it a sandwich?”
“This may be bigger than sandwiches,” Axey whispered.
Far beyond the lanterns moved a long, shadowy creature. Stars shone inside its chest, then faded. Wherever it passed, another light disappeared.
Coatl's warning buttons glowed. Nebula Johnny raised a moon shield over the heroes. The Dragon Couple flew together along its edge, guiding the smaller friends toward shelter.
The Skykeeper wanted to close the sky gate before the creature reached it.
“Then it will be trapped outside,” Opal said.
“And our stars will be safe.”
Lolo watched the creature pause beside a very small star. It curled around the light before swallowing it.
“It looks cold,” she said.
Opal asked the Skykeeper to wait while they learned more. They would keep the shield in place. Nobody had to stand unprotected to ask a question.
Unique Pink made a lantern on a long ribbon. Axey carried it to the edge of the safe path and set it down.
The Star Eater turned.

illustration.alt: Opal holds her sloth lovey Lolo while reading inside the purple galaxy tent.

paragraphs: Its face was enormous and tired. It lowered its head to the lantern, but did not take it.
“That one is warm,” it whispered.
“Are the stars not warm?” Opal asked.
“Only for a moment.”
The creature had lost the little light that guided it home. It had followed bigger and bigger stars, hoping one would fill the dark place inside its chest. None had stayed.
The Skykeeper lowered her basket.
“I thought you wanted to empty our sky.”
“I wanted not to be lost,” the creature said.
“You still have to give the stars back,” Opal told it.
The Star Eater bowed its head. “I don't know how.”
Opal studied the dim points inside its shadowy chest. They were not gone. They were scattered, each following a different path.
Finley drew the pattern in her notebook. Cinny found a repeating shape, and Axey recognized it as a route: a trail of little stars leading beyond the sky gate.
The Skykeeper opened her basket. Its moonlight formed the beginning of a bridge.
“I can guide the stars,” she said. “But they need something to follow.”
Opal placed her gemstone beside the lantern. It glowed warmly, joining its light to Nebula Johnny's shield. Lolo stood close enough for Opal to feel her soft shoulder.
One by one, the stars lifted from the creature's chest. Water Kitty caught their reflections in floating bubbles. The Dragon Couple escorted each pair back into the sky.
Langston kept count.
“Seventeen, eighteen, an extremely sparkly nineteen—”
“That's the same star,” Finley said.
“An encore.”
At last only one faint light remained: small, uneven, and almost hidden beneath the creature's heart.
The Star Eater looked down in surprise.
“My home light.”
“It was easier to see when the others had room to go,” Lolo said.
The Skykeeper opened the gate. This time the creature could follow its own light through it.
Before leaving, it asked whether it might visit again.
“Yes,” Opal said. “You can follow the lanterns. You don't have to swallow them.”
Above the galaxy tent, every star shone in its own place. Langston tucked an emergency sandwich into his pocket.
“Just in case the next visitor is hungry for ordinary reasons.”
Opal laughed, and Lolo leaned against her beneath the restored sky.
The End.
